name: Covenant Extraction
title: Covenant Extraction
answer: Covenant extraction is the work of pulling the specific terms and conditions out of loan and bond documentation and turning them into structured data. In fixed income and credit risk it covers maintenance and incurrence covenants, baskets, carve-outs, definitions of EBITDA, leverage ratios, restricted payments, liens and change of control triggers. The output feeds covenant monitoring, compliance checks, credit models and portfolio surveillance rather than replacing the analyst who reads the document. It sits between legal document review and credit analytics, and the unit of work is usually one credit agreement or indenture at a time.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Covenant extraction is the work of pulling the specific terms and conditions out of loan and bond documentation and turning them into structured data. In fixed income and credit risk it covers maintenance and incurrence covenants, baskets, carve-outs, definitions of EBITDA, leverage ratios, restricted payments, liens and change of control triggers. The output feeds covenant monitoring, compliance checks, credit models and portfolio surveillance rather than replacing the analyst who reads the document. It sits between legal document review and credit analytics, and the unit of work is usually one credit agreement or indenture at a time.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is the document itself, typically a PDF or a scanned credit agreement, indenture or amendment, often hundreds of pages with cross-references and defined terms. Extraction runs on document parsing and layout tools, optical character recognition where scans are poor, and a store of the parsed text with section and page anchors so every extracted term can be traced back. Large language models handle the reading and classification, usually with a retrieval layer over the document and a schema that fixes the fields to be filled. Output lands in a database or spreadsheet that credit and portfolio teams already use, with the source clause kept alongside each value.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with identifying the document type and the sections that matter, then locating each covenant and its definitions. Models extract the clause text, the threshold, the test date, the basket size and the exceptions, and a reviewer checks the result against the source. Because defined terms carry most of the meaning, the pipeline resolves references such as Consolidated EBITDA or Permitted Liens before a value is recorded. Quality is measured by field-level accuracy against a human-coded sample, and disagreements are fed back to improve prompts, schemas and parsing rules.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Covenant terms are contractual and can affect pricing, waivers and default decisions, so provenance matters: each extracted value should point to the exact clause and page it came from. Access to the underlying documents is usually restricted by licence and confidentiality, and extracted data may be shared only within the permitted scope. Errors can misstate leverage or headroom, so a named reviewer signs off before the data is used in reporting or monitoring. Audit trails, versioning of the document and of the extraction run, and a clear record of model and prompt changes are the usual controls.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Coverage is widening from a handful of standard covenant types to the full set of baskets, carve-outs and definitional chains that appear in real agreements. Expect tighter links between extracted terms and live monitoring, so a breach signal can be traced to the clause that produced it. Benchmarks and shared schemas are likely to standardise how covenant fields are named and compared across deals. The open questions are how much review remains necessary and how to keep extraction accurate as documents and market practice change.
